utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start hearing the evidence, Judge Fluegge is, for a mixed urgent personal and authorised Tribunal business, is unable to sit this day, therefore is of short duration. And Judge Moloto and myself are satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to continue today. So therefore we're sitting as it's colloquially called Rule 15 bis. I was informed that there were no preliminaries, therefore the witness could be escorted into the courtroom. I, meanwhile, use the time for the following: On the 28th of December of last year, the Prosecution filed their confidential 92 ter motion concerning Witness RM157. The Defence has requested on the 11th of January of this year an extension of seven days to respond to the motion which was particularly voluminous, 215 pages. And the witness is scheduled to testify in the week of the 28th of January, 2012 [sic], and the request is granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Selmanovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand? I'll speak a few words so that the system can be tested.

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: I hear it perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- Mrs. Selmanovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, I'd like to remind you that the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony is still binding upon you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue where we were, but I think, Mr. Traldi, the last thing we discussed was the addition of 65 ter 28614 to the 65 ter exhibit list. I think we had dealt with 28613. And, Mr. Stojanovic, you would consider your position again, whether you'd still oppose this list of names to be added to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not object because we'll be using that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let me just try to -- you wanted to have it added to the 65 ter list and you wanted to tender it, Mr. Traldi, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'd renew my application to have it admitted at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 28614.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P726, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am. Do you recall when we left off on Monday --

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall when we left off on Monday that we were discussing a list of names that you and your friend Muniba Colic had put together.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I just have one further question about that list for the clarity of the record. Did the two of you draft the list together before you met with the Office of the Prosecutor or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd ask that the court officer please call up 65 ter 19610. This is a document which identifies itself as emanating from the cantonal court in Sarajevo and is dated September 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, ma'am, before we discuss this document, in paragraph 23 of P717 at page 7 of both the English and the B/C/S, you talk about the exhumation of a grave-site at Ivan Polje. Were you present for that exhumation?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present over three days. For two days they kept attempting to find something but nothing happened, but on the third day toward the end of their work they started finding remains. They were -- we were on the surface and once they had completed with their work, the people from the commission, they asked us to come up closer and they asked me, Now, first of all, Madam, can you tell me what your child wore? And my child had worn on that day a T-shirt which was striped red and white. And then he had also jeans and a chain around his neck and then they said, Oh, all right then. So then they took a body-bag. They opened it. They said, Don't anyone touch anything with their hands. We will show you everything. And then they showed me the clothes and I recognised them and then they kept searching for something, and then I asked them, Well, why is this bullet there? And they said, Well, Madam, you see this bullet here next to the T-shirt, you can see that it's torn in the back so -- and then they told me, You know, your son was shot in the head and in the chest and such-like. And I really can't say much more. And I state here with full responsibility that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, ma'am, at the bottom of page 2 in the English, this report describes the scene at that grave-site. I'm going to read to you three brief excerpts. I'd ask if they accurately describe what you were able to observe that day. The report says: "Garbage is strewn everywhere." It says: "Part of the elongated round shape of a minaret can be seen among the bodies." And they conclude that: "The remains of a destroyed mosque are located there." And that's at Ivan Polje. Does that accurately describe the scene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we enlarge the portion you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, we can't see it; that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's too small. And it looks as if not the same text is there in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the text in the B/C/S starts at the bottom of page 2 but continues at the top of page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, ma'am, again for the record, does that accurately describe what you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's accurate. There was some kind of meadow and that was used as a garbage dump. And they found parts of the mosque, some debris, and a lot of time had passed. We didn't know anything about what had happened to them, but because my husband and son and the others were there we reported to the commission that was searching for the people and they tried to do their work. And whenever we went to Sokolac we always visited this site; it wasn't too far from the main road. Yes, it's the truth. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, ma'am, I have three more very specific questions for you about this exhumation. First, were the names of people in this exhumation report read to you in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you recognise them as people you last saw on 22 September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the report refers to someone named Osman Sestic. Do you believe that person's name to be Osman Sestic as in your statement and in the list you provided to us?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is Osman Sejtic [phoen] and there is also Osman Selmanovic, so please go ahead, just ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am, I think that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 19610 for admission as the next Prosecution public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P727, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P727 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And finally, ma'am, I want to go back to what happened on Metaljka on 22 September 1992. On Monday you mentioned a soldier named Milenko Koprivica. Did any of the people from Novoseoci who were there know him or his family?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan you said but I didn't get the last name. What did you say it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Milenko Koprivica, ma'am. I'm sorry if I'm pronouncing it poorly.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Koprivica -- Nikola Koprivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did any of the people from Novoseoci know him or his family?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't know his family, but I knew him by site because I went with my neighbour Namira Ocuz, and his son and this Namira woman's son, they went to school together. So, she asked him, Please, my child is 15 years old, please go and get him. And she mentioned Milenko Koprivica then. She shook hands with him and that's how she asked him to do this favour for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Her child was 15, is that Damir, who's mentioned in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Damir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And how old was your son at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son was 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you also ask to have him stay with you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I begged. It didn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened for the Chamber in your own words?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all there at Metaljka and we were supposed to be sent to Sarajevo by bus. They ordered and said that they would come and get us, and I went to my child to get him with me. But they said, No, Madam, you have to go to Sarajevo, and your husband and your children and the others, they will have to stay here for a work drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then, Mrs. Selmanovic, you describe in paragraph 20 of P717 how after you got on the bus it took you to Hresa and then you walked to Sarajevo. Now, your father was on the bus too. Was he capable of walking to Sarajevo himself?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And how did he arrive in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he couldn't walk because he had been beaten and he could not move. So when we got off the bus, we took him off the bus. We carried him. A woman and I carried him together but then we couldn't get very far. And then a neighbour of mine, she had a blanket or something. She gave it to us. And there were some soldiers who escorted us. They also brought some floor carpeting and we put him on that. And then we tried to move on from Hresa, but they kept telling us, You can't leave this here. You have to carry it with you. Now they said to us, Don't you leave this here and you will reach barricades. We didn't know anything about this, but there was something that was placed across the road. We crossed that, some kind of barrier. And then there was shooting but we didn't -- we just fled everywhere, you know, all the way we knew how. And there was shooting. I was in the middle of the road. There was a neighbour who said, Why don't you -- I won't leave him, don't worry. I'll stay here with you, although there was shooting all around. And then two soldiers came by. I stayed there with my father for quite a while. Then two other soldiers came and then they helped us and brought us -- carried us into a house. Now, when they carried my father into the house, I saw that there were some women, our women, there, with small children --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then from there we took my father in a car because they came with a car there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. I have one very last specific question for you, Mrs. Selmanovic. Did your father continue to live in Sarajevo for the rest of the war?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father died on the 12th day when I arrived there in 1992, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Ms. Selmanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Selmanovic, I only have a few questions for you, but before I start I would like just to say on behalf of the entire Defence team that we're deeply sorry for everything that you had gone through and for your loss. I would ask you to look at the document we saw a moment ago together; that is, document P726 now. And you will see before you, Mrs. Selmanovic, a list that was discussed a little earlier. Could you tell us how long after the exhumation in 2002 was this list compiled. Or, let me put it this way: When did you compile this list together with your friend?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did it now, but I think I had it from -- I had another one from before. I couldn't remember all the names. There was Pasic, Celo; and Colic, Hasib; Adem Catic; Hodzic, Ismet Hodzic. Those four I could not remember right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that after the exhumation on one occasion you sent to the Prosecutor another list that did not include all of these names; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this list -- you drafted this list before you came to The Hague for this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I ask this is so that you can help us. Could you tell us who from this list was not from your village?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was Amir Selmanovic, the son of Memis. There are two Selmanovics here, but I'm referring to the one who is the son of Memis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we did not understand each other well. Which of the people on this list were not from Novoseoci before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of all the people here, they were all people who lived in Novoseoci. The Selmanovics, the Ocuz, the Karic, the Sestics, and the Kabas. The Pasic family, these are in-laws, sons-in-laws or brothers-in-laws, our husbands' relatives, also Vatres, Bajro, who lived with his sister. They were all ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ismet Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ismet Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he with his family?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, he was staying with the Karic family together with his Colics.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did they live before 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lived in Kovalj, where Nezim Colic was. These were his uncles and his relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far away is that village from Novoseoci?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps some 8 to 10 kilometres. I couldn't really tell you exactly. And this is in the direction of Rogatica, Kovani [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber a little more about the exhumation site at Ivan Polje.

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's on Ivan Polje. If you go from our village, it's to the left towards Hrabro, and it's not far from the road, perhaps a hundred metres or so at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far is that site from Metaljka, the place where you parted from your dear ones?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a kilometre or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the body of your late husband, was there anyone else from this list who had not been found in that mass grave?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my husband's remains were found, but on the other side of this grave, and it was only last year. But, yes, one more thing I want to say: Amir Selmanovic is the only one who is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And his body has not been recovered to this day?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, not to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know when those people were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't know when they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nor do you know who killed them?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not known.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The people who arrived in your village, whom you named to the best of your recollection as having been there that day, were they members of the police, of the reserve police, or the army?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw soldiers. As for the police, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How do you tell such people apart? How do you know someone was from the army?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not as if I belong to the army. I saw the army there that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you base your conclusion on, to say that they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they had olive-drab and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who is Momcilo Pajic and had you known him before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a surveyor in Sokolac before the war, land surveyor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he leave his job at some point in time and left to Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he gathered all of us together at the meadow near Metaljka, that's when he went to Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did he stay there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 20 and 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to ask you is this: The 20 to 30 minutes during which -- is that the time during which you went to fetch your father?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned with him, had the man you just mentioned returned from Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had. He ordered that all women, children, and those physically unfit were to go to Sarajevo, whereas all able-bodied men were to remain behind for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After you received that information, how much later did the buses arrive which took you to Hresa?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After some 20 to 30 minutes, that's when the buses arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you have to walk from the place you were at Metaljka to the place where the buses were?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't -- well, we walked for less than 15 minutes. It was close, but I had to support my father and another woman helped me. Later on my husband helped me to put him in a wheelbarrow to carry him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could there please be pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the interpreters asked for a pause between question and answer. And, Ms. Selmanovic, would you also wait for a second after Mr. Stojanovic has finished his question before you answer it. Could you please repeat the last part of your answer. What we read in the transcript is: "Later on my husband helped me to put him in a wheelbarrow to carry him." What did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I brought my father to the bus -- we did, actually, and then he helped me put my father on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who told your husband that he wasn't allowed on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the soldiers, although I don't know him. He had an olive-drab uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly sit closer to the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were those buses civilian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, could you come a bit closer to the microphone, please. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May we continue, Ms. Selmanovic? My question was this: To the best of your recollection, were those buses civilian?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whose buses they were. I didn't presume they were civilian. I was in a state of shock. We were just told to go on and that the women and children should board, and we put my father on the floor of the bus. I sat in one of the seats and my father was beside me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P720 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, let me ask you this,

utterances.speaker: MS. SELMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your husband remain on the road once you set off or was he taken away before the buses moved away?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband stayed on the road. He was kicked out of the bus and that's the last I saw of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before you is a death certificate which you handed over a short while ago to the Prosecution. I wanted to ask you this only: In 1999, what was the basis for this death certificate to be issued to you concerning your husband?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband used to work and I was entitled to his pension. I was trying to exercise that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was an administrative procedure or proceedings before a court in order to declare him dead because at that time there were still no such documents in existence?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were proceedings. We had to go back to the death register office, and only after we have obtained all the papers then I could conclude the procedure concerning his pension.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this document we have the date, month, and year, as well as hour of death, the 22nd of September, 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who provided that information to the court as the date of his death?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, alongside some witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you didn't know if he was killed that day. You provided that piece of information based on the fact that you saw him on that day for the last time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, on the English version of the certificate, I do not see the time. Can you please guide us to where the time is on that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version, Your Honour, it reads on the left-hand side: "Date of death, day, month, year, and hour." So we have "hour" in English instead of time. However, the rest of that line does not specify the precise time. We only have the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, and I do see the word "hour," but I don't see what hour it was when he died. But the question to the witness was: How do you -- you gave the hour of death to the authorities. I'm saying what hour is this that she gave? Do you have it in the B/C/S? Is the hour mentioned in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, neither in the B/C/S nor in the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is only in the left-hand side column that I read out to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, but you can't follow that question up because, in any case, the hour is not given -- the hour of death is not given. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Thank you for your assistance and clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you, Ms. Selmanovic, whether you provided that piece of information based on the fact that you saw him then for the last time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So many years after those tragic events, you still don't know when he was killed precisely; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also don't know or you have no information about whether he was taken to work somewhere and then killed?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information, whether he was taken to any kind of labour. It's just that I saw him in 1992 for the last time, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, primarily the prosecutor's office, did they summon you to provide a statement in the proceedings conducted against certain persons with relation to this event?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned the people you saw on the 22nd of September, 1992, in your village to them?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at one other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P718, Your Honours. Could we have the second page in both versions, the last paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a document from the 2nd Romanija Brigade Command of the 22nd of August, 1992. Mrs. Selmanovic, you were asked about it during proofing. In this report sent to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command by the 2nd Romanija Brigade, it reads: "Within this territory in the villages of Micivode, Raktitnica, Kramer Selo and Novoseoci, there is a certain number of extremists who are peaceful for now. They are not causing problems to the Serbian population but we are keeping them under control." Let me ask you this first: In the proximity of your village --

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are the villages of Micivode, Raktitnica, and Kramer Selo close to your village?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Micivode is towards Han Pijesak. Raktitnica is towards Rogatica. They are not close to our area. The closest villages to ours are Jelosaljevici [phoen], Pavacici [phoen] and other Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the type of guard that was held in the village in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with it because my husband and others informed them. They would come and see my father and tell him that there were no problems and that they could continue living and working there. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who organised the village guards, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village guards, I don't know if anyone stood guard. They just came and spoke to our people, telling them that there was no need to go and to live there. As for any guards, I'm not clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any point in time when the authorities in Rogatica asked that the military -- the men fit for military service be enlisted into the army?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your late husband, did he receive a draft call in 1992 at any point of time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at document - it's a 65 ter document - number 06862.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd just put on the record at this time that we haven't gotten a list of documents from the Defence to use with this witness. This was initially on our list so I won't object to this one being used, but in the future it would be good if we got some notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In any case, Your Honour, if the omission was on our part, we accept that. According to the information I am receiving, we informed the Prosecution that we will only be using such documents that are on their list. Not a single document that we wanted to rely on was uploaded into e-court by us. This document, too, is on the Prosecution list. That's what we included in our e-mail sent to them, I believe. If I am wrong, I stand to be corrected of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, if documents are on your list, the purpose of notifying the Prosecution about the use of certain documents seems to fall away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and that's why I hadn't objected to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I didn't received the communication Mr. Stojanovic mentions, but I'm sure it's a one-time occurrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from that, apparently the Defence does not intend to use any document that is not on your list. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before us is a document of the SRK command dated the 27th of July, 1992. Let us look at the second paragraph where, among other things, we read: "In the village of Novoseoci to the south of Sokolac by some 5 to 6 kilometres (Glasinacko Polje) there was a hand-over of arms and lethal assets by the Muslim population to representatives of the 2nd Romanija Brigade. The hand-over was conducted as previously agreed and it is believed that not all of the weapons had been handed over." Ms. Selmanovic, do you know anything about the existence of weapons in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know that they came and gathered all of the people. They discussed who had what weapons to hand over. People had some hunting rifles and that's what was handed over. That's what my husband told me. The weapons were handed over. I have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document as a Defence exhibit. It's 65 ter 06862.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D130 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Selmanovic, I will end this with one additional question. After the war and the implementation of the new laws, your house was returned to you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but it's in no shape of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you own that house?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and my children and I own it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did people return to Novoseoci?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people of Novoseoci are asking for donations. I don't know if they're doing this through the Sokolac municipality, but if you ask me whether anyone has returned to live there, reside there, no, they didn't. They are just looking after their property there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Selmanovic, thank you. And I apologise if my questions caused you any sorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Traldi, is there any need to -- for questions -- further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour, and I'll be done in just a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Ma'am, at temporary transcript page 20 today's transcript Mr. Stojanovic asked you about weapons in Novoseoci. I have just one very simple question for you about this. Did you know of any weapons which were kept in your village after the surrender of weapons in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At temporary transcript page 18, Mr. Stojanovic asked you about guards and you responded discussing people who had come to your village and said everything would be okay and people didn't have to leave. When you answered, were you discussing Serb guards or Bosniak guards?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Serb guards, Serbs came, but I didn't say anything about guards or patrols. I knew nothing of that. I didn't know that there were any patrols. I didn't know anything about that nor did I hear it from my husband nor anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at temporary transcript page 11, Mr. Stojanovic asked you if you knew when the men from Novoseoci had been killed or by whom. Can you simply tell us, when you last saw your husband and son alive, were they free or were they under someone else's control?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To that I can only say this: All of us, all the other villagers, me and my child and my husband, we were all on a meadow together. And from there my child remained but my husband, his -- he helped my father, but as for them, I know nothing of their fate after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you last saw them, could they go freely wherever they chose or was there someone restricting them?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their movement was up until some time in May when people still worked. Later on, we, the women, would go to Sokolac from time to time but there were no obstacles. Others would come and say --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, ma'am, but I'm asking specifically about when you last saw your husband and son on September 22nd. And at that time, were they free or were they under someone else's control?

utterances.speaker: MUNIRA SELMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I last saw my husband at Metaljka, this meadow, when he was left there, how could I know whether he was free or not when there was -- there were troops all around him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Ms. Selmanovic, since the Chamber has no further questions for you and as I understand there's no request for further questions by the Defence, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming and having answered questions about past events which may have been difficult for you to think back of. And I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, we are ready to call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Bibles, have you explained Rule 15 bis to the witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so the witness is aware that tomorrow there'll be three Judges again?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, I was thinking of another Rule. No, I did not advise him of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not? Then I'll briefly explain to him the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in, I will take up a quick matter, and that is we do intend to tender a reduced number of associated exhibits. We would propose that it would be beneficial to defer that application until the conclusion of the witness's testimony if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll deal with it at the end just as about the admission of the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rose. Please be seated. Mr. Rose, if I address you as "Mr. Rose," that is because that is what the Chamber does with all witnesses, that is, without titles, without ranks. It is not out of disrespect for the titles and the ranks you may hold. Ms. Bibles, if you're ready, please start your examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you tell us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Hugh Michael Rose.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, General, you served as commander of the UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina from the 5th of January, 1994, until the 23rd of January, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Based on your work in that time-period, have you previously presented evidence regarding your observations and experiences here at ICTY and at the International Court of Criminal Justice?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: On three separate occasions I have done so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You have also authored a book about your experiences which is titled: "Fighting for Peace"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review a statement dated 26 March 2009 as well as certain associated exhibits which consolidates the elements of your evidence into one statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And since we're both native English speakers, I will attempt myself to pause between question and answer and slow down and would ask you to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that page 1 of the English version of 65 ter 28619 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General, once the document is on the screen before you, I would ask that you view the signature at the bottom of the page and indicate whether you recognise that signature.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that we now go to page 53 of the English document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And likewise, do you recognise the signature on this page?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And whose is that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As you reviewed the document, did you also note initials on every page of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And whose initials are those?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: They are mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In reviewing the statement, did you note any changes or corrections to the document?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I would bring your attention, Your Honours, to paragraphs 150, 151, and 167.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you note that there were paragraphs which had a date of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yeah, I didn't notice that at the time but obviously it should read "1994."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would simply note those corrections on those three paragraphs. They appear to be typographical errors.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With these corrections in mind, if you were asked about these matters, would you today give the same answers that are contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I would indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Having taken the solemn oath, do you affirm that the information in this document is accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, having established the foundational requirements necessary, we do tender 28619 into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A number will be assigned to it. In view of the objections raised by the Defence the Chamber will decide at the end of the testimony about admission. Mr. Registrar, the number to be assigned to the witness statement would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P728, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P728 is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I read a brief public summary of the witness's written testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General Sir Michael Rose was the commander of the United Nations protection forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina from January 1994 through January of 1995. General Rose arrived in Sarajevo on the 23rd of January 1994 with a mission to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and to attempt to bring a peaceful resolution of the war. He found in Sarajevo a city that had no lights, water, or electricity. He was briefed on the sniping and indiscriminate shelling by the Bosnian Serbs of civilians in the city centre, including the very recent deaths of children who had been out tobogganing in the snow. During his tenure, General Rose met frequently with General Mladic, Radovan Karadzic, and others in the Bosnian Serb leadership. General Rose regularly raised issuing of sniping in Sarajevo as well as issues of freedom of movement and access for humanitarian convoys in these meetings. General Rose observed that the Bosnian Serbs blocked humanitarian aid or utilities as a means of achieving political ends and/or in response to Bosnian or NATO actions elsewhere. After the 5 February 1994 shelling of Markale Market in Sarajevo, General Rose acted quickly to implement a cease-fire by setting a 20-kilometre Total Exclusion Zone for heavy weapons. The cease-fire was largely effective and held for most of the year. Sniping continued but in August of 1994 the factions agreed to an anti-sniping agreement which was followed by a decrease in sniping for the following weeks. As autumn 1994 came to an end, the situation in Bosnia deteriorated with an increase in shelling and sniping incidents in Sarajevo and restrictions on utilities and the flow of humanitarian aid until a cessation of hostilities agreement was signed by the parties on the 31st of December 1994. General Rose maintained a relationship with the Bosnian Serb army and General Mladic during which he observed that the decision-making in the Bosnian Serb army was done at the highest levels and that General Mladic and Karadzic were at the peak of the pyramid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's only now that the French translation finished. Would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Were at the peak of the pyramid of control of the Bosnian Serb forces. General Rose notes that General Mladic had the ability to control the shelling and sniping in Sarajevo and that the siege was used by Bosnian Serb leaders to exert pressure on the United Nations, the international community, and the Bosnian Muslims. General Rose recognised that nothing happened militarily without General Mladic's knowledge or authorisation. Your Honours, this concludes the summary. May I proceed with questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will note that we estimated two hours for direct; we will be substantially less than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General, let's first turn our attention to your meetings and negotiations with the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership. Could you please describe for us whether there were consistent topics discussed throughout 1994 in these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were consistently the following subjects discussed: The demilitarisation of Sarajevo, following the withdrawal of heavy weapons; the running of humanitarian aid convoys to the various enclaves, including Sarajevo; and the maintaining of the utilities to the various enclaves as well; and of course the ultimate aim was to bring about a cessation of hostilities long-term which would bring about a peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As a result of your meetings and interactions on these topics, did you develop an overview of the political/military situation as it existed in the beginning of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did indeed. At that time the Serbs controlled approximately 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including territory which ran up to within 75 metres of the Bosnian government Presidency in Sarajevo. They were the dominant military force in that country throughout 1994, and therefore they were in a position to control most of the convoy runs to the 2.7 million people who were dependent on humanitarian aid throughout that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: During 1994, did the political and military situation change?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The political and military situation changed dramatically in 1994, with the bringing about of an agreement known as the Washington Accord between the Croatian warring party and the Bosnian government warring party, say two out of the three warring parties had now formed Federations, and that tilted the strategic balance, both militarily and politically against the Bosnian Serbs. And from that moment on, it was evident to the United Nations - and indeed to the Bosnian Serbs - that they were in a declining political and military situation, deteriorating possibly I should say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Given your experience in the meetings and negotiations during this shift, did you develop an understanding of the ultimate territorial objectives of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did indeed, and the conclusion we came to that they wished to have contiguous territory as part of the Republika Srpska; and secondly, that that should include parts of Sarajevo and that the total proportion would be 51 per cent in favour of the Serbs, 49 per cent in favour of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you determine whether there were areas in and around Sarajevo that the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted to remain wholly Serb?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: In particular, Globuvica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Likewise, were there areas of Bosnia that you determined the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted to be wholly Serb?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: They were determined to retain possession of Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You have described --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this would be paragraph 20 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: -- that the facilitation of the delivery of humanitarian aid was a mission of UNPROFOR. Did you observe whether it was in the Bosnian Serb interests to facilitate these convoys in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, the Bosnian Serbs clearly regarded the running of humanitarian aid convoys to the enclaves as contrary to their strategic aims of bringing political pressure to bear on the Bosnian government to sign up to peace on Serb terms rather than on their terms, the Bosnian government terms, so they were using the flow of aid very much as an instrument with which to bring pressure to bear on the Bosnian government to sign up to peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you observe what tactics were employed in this process?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, there were many tactics employed which ranged from the physical blocking of convoys on the road to bureaucratic measures which required the listing of the manifest down to the minutest detail. And, of course, inevitably, if they discovered that, for example, there was one more tin of baked beans had been delivered than required - and this is an illustrative example - then the convoy would be turned back. It was impossible basically to comply with all the requests that had been laid upon the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Am I speaking too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are close to that, and if you have some compassion with transcribers and interpreters, I would invite you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you raise your concerns about these tactics in your meetings?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could bring up 65 ter 08162, and this would initially be page 1 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To the extent possible, could you also indicate in relation to what part of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Paragraph 182, Your Honours, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you please look at this page and let us know if you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I would specifically ask you to look at paragraph 3 before we pull up the next page.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Okay, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With respect, and I believe it's on - thank you - page 2 of the B/C/S version. With respect to subsection (b), does this accurately depict your statements as you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could we now look at page 2 of the English version. And again, specifically directing your attention to the remainder of paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all extra microphones be switched off, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Does this document accurately describe the discussion as you recall it on the 12th of December?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It does indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 08162.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whom should I look at to know whether there are any objections? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P729, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P729 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We can remove the document from the screen at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Given the situation that you describe with the convoys in this meeting towards the end of 1994, were you aware of what impact that was having on the people who lived in the enclaves, in the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was having a very negative impact. They were daily dependent on not only food but also medical supplies for their survival, particularly during the winter months, and the halting of the convoys are meant that they suffered almost immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd like now to shift your attention to Sarajevo. In paragraph 201 of your statement, in the context of the shelling of Sarajevo by the Bosnian Serbs you state: "The usual response from the Bosnian Serb leadership to protest of shelling was that they were responding to attacks by the Bosnian Muslim army." You acknowledge that the Bosnian forces were firing out from within Sarajevo. Then you state: "The disproportionality of the Bosnian Serb response, however, undermines the credibility of this justification." General, could you please articulate why you considered the Bosnian Serb response to be disproportionate?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: One only had to look at a suburb like Dobrinja which had been totally destroyed. People were living in the cellars in order to survive. If even a cat walked across the street, it was engaged by artillery. The response was demonstrably disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, may I take it that disproportionately should be disproportionality?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Court how effective the February 1994 cease-fire was in reducing the shelling in Sarajevo for the remainder of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The bringing about of the withdrawal of heavy weapons from Sarajevo transformed the lives of the people of Sarajevo and gave them some hope that there would be a return to long-term peace, a hope which was sadly disappointed at the end of 1994. But during the summer of 1994, electricity was restored. Water was restored. The trams started to run again. Major convoys came over land from Europe into Sarajevo to replenish the warehouses and stocks of food. Life seemed to be returning to normal for the people of Sarajevo as a result of that cessation or withdrawal of heavy weapons from around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: When negotiating either for this cease-fire, the February cease-fire, or later the anti-sniping agreement, were you aware of what level within the Bosnian Serb army made the decisions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: All decisions were made at the top in Pale by both the civil and the military side, one represented by Mr. Karadzic and the other by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General, given what you've described, that the negotiations or the negotiating was at the highest level, did this allow you to form a judgement about the ability of the senior levels of the Bosnian Serb army command to control the level of sniping in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: In our view, there was absolute control of every single sniper and he would not have been allowed to open fire unless he'd been duly authorised and the reverse was equally true.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In your statement, to go back to the cease-fire, in paragraph 44, you describe reaching the agreement on the cease-fire. You further describe in the following paragraph, 45, that you tested the cease-fire and that your observation was that the shelling stopped. Can you, however, briefly describe for us your degree of certainty both at the time and with -- your perspective now, the degree of certainty in the UN's ability to determine whether the heavy weapons were actually moved out of the 20-kilometre area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Of course at the time the UN were under no illusion that both sides had fully withdrawn heavy weapons out of the 20-kilometre circle around Sarajevo or in the case of the Bosnian government forces taken them out of use. But the fact that they were not using them is what mattered. And of course, on the Bosnian Serb side, they merely handed in the out-of-date weapons which they had ceased to require to the weapon collecting points. It was certain, and we had evidence by discovering at least one T55 tank hidden, that they had concealed most of their heavy weapons for future use.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please bring 65 ter exhibit 19674 to the screen. And this would be page 1 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to ... ?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: This is one of the non-associated exhibits that we indicated we would be using.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In reviewing the first page of this document, it proposes methods of appearing to comply with the cease-fire and yet maintain heavy weapons within the zone. Are the terms of this proposal consistent with your experiences that you've just described regarding the detection of Bosnian Serb heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That very much reflects our view.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'll ask that we go to -- I believe it's page -- well, that is the page. Your Honours, I -- the Prosecution tenders 19674.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P730, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P730 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Directing your attention now to the time-period of August 1994, after the anti-sniping agreement was signed, was there an improvement in sniping in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was a distinct and immediate improvement, although in the end that agreement was not adhered to by either side and the situation deteriorated. But at least for a month there was a perceptible improvement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Shifting your attention now to the enclaves, in your statement - and this would be paragraphs 65 through 101 - you describe the Bosnian Serb offensive on Gorazde. Could you describe for us where the negotiations for a global peace in the country were when this offensive began?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The UN at that time were engaged with both the warring parties about bringing about a long-term cessation of hostilities, and the argument between the two parties was whether to make Gorazde and what was happening there part of the global cease-fire plan or whether Gorazde should be resolved first and then the global plan addressed. The Bosnian government side wanted Gorazde to be resolved before embarking on long-term discussions about a permanent cease-fire. The Serb side wanted the opposite, and it was almost impossible to get any agreement. And it was at this point that presumably to put pressure on the Bosnian government side that the Bosnian Serbs launched a [indiscernible] offensive into the enclave of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you have opportunities to communicate with General Mladic during the Gorazde operation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: On a number of occasions we spoke by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you explain for us a little bit more - I believe it's in paragraph 86 - how your calls to the Bosnian Serb leadership resulted in your being on the phone with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think a little explanation may be required. The Bosnian Serb, and indeed all Soviet Warsaw Pact countries tended to lay telephone wires as well as use radio communications. And therefore all messages that we passed to General Mladic tended to go down the telephone communications and they laid wires to their front line. And we discovered that whatever telephone number we dialled in Pale, somehow we always ended up talking directly to General Mladic and they had merely switched their exchange, telephone exchange to enable that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you describe for us in these conversations with General Mladic if you could ascertain where he was physically located?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Not really, but it was evident from TV coverage that he was located around Gorazde itself leading the attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In your statement you've set out examples of General Mladic's control of events on the ground and specifically I direct attention to paragraph 85. Did you have any examples indicating that General Mladic had anything less than total control of the Bosnian Serb forces during the Gorazde offensive?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Absolutely not. He was in total control, as one would have expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether or not General Mladic was in the battle-field arena on the 10th of April of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: He certainly would have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please bring 65 ter 08996 to our screens. This is a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Branko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you know there should be no consultations during the hearing. If you would approach Mr. Mladic and find out what causes him to ask for a time-out without further discussions, which should take place during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, would you please report to the Chamber the situation. Yes, we'll continue. Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just I was briefly instructed by my client --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- how to follow the testimony of General Rose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it should not be done during the hearing but during the breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This may be clear to Mr. Mladic now. May I remind him of the rules which apply in this courtroom. Ms. Bibles, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to General Mladic's statements in paragraph 7 of this document, specifically where he describes his -- '"The Turks must disappear from these areas.'" Is this position stated in this document consistent with General Mladic in his stated intentions to you with respect to the offensive?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: General Mladic at the time was telling us that he was recovering the lost territory which had previously been occupied by the Serbs and 1993, I think, had been driven from their homes, that that was the limit of his aim. And at the time we tended to believe that they only wanted to advance as far as the old Serb areas, not going into the Muslim parts of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers just before there was a short interruption. Mr. Rose, you were asked whether you were aware of whether or not General Mladic was in the battle-field arena on the 10th of April of 1994. Your answer was: "He certainly would have been," which -- what makes you believe or conclude that he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UN of course had no intelligence-gathering capability and it was -- we were not being passed any intelligence either by NATO. Therefore, we had to assume a number of things, and it would be characteristic of General Mladic to have personally led the attacks himself and not to have absented himself when a major offensive was taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was an assessment on the basis of you gained experience with the way in which General Mladic exercised command and control; is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He preferred to lead from the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 08996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P731, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: General, your statement sets out through several paragraphs, calling for NATO air-strikes in response to the Bosnian Serb offensive in Gorazde. Did your working relationship with General Mladic change as a result of those air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It changed dramatically for the following six weeks or maybe two months. Even during the discussions in Geneva where the Serb party was involved he refused to speak directly to any UNPROFOR personnel and channelled all his questions through Colonel Tolimir, who was his aid, military aide. Also, I think, they began to take the view that the UN were now engaging in a war against Serbia, although we tried to persuade them that we were merely enforcing passages of convoys, maintaining the integrity of the withdrawal of heavy weapons agreement or the agreement to demilitarise the zone on Mount Igman. We were not waging war. I suspect that they began to see we, the international community, were beginning to take sides at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you tell us generally whether the Bosnian Serb forces took action against UN employees and humanitarian workers as a result of the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Immediately following air-strikes, the Bosnian Serbs would halt all convoys, seize convoys that were on their territory at the time, and take hostages. That was the normal practice following an air-strike.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that 65 ter 14676 be brought to our screens. And, Your Honours, 14676 pertains to paragraph 96 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you please review this document with particular attention to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: With respect to General Mladic's reference to the use of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations for anti-aircraft combat, what do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, I guess that they by placing hostages around their positions, military positions, they would hope to deter NATO air-strikes against those positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 14676.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to find a date on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It appears to be undated, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P732, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I set that document a little bit in context? The UN never had any intention of carrying out massive air-strikes. We merely used minimum force to enforce the passage of a convoy, et cetera. The intelligence that the Bosnian Serb side therefore had that NATO was going to launch massive strikes was faulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We can remove this document from the screen, although, Your Honours, I will note that paragraph 1 of the order list the 19th of April of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether the document is of that date is different, but at least some context in terms of time is given here. Mr. Registrar, the number would be ... ? Oh, yes, no, you've given the number already. It's P732 and is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Based on your experiences and observations, were you able to draw conclusions as to General Mladic's ability to control the events on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well certainly he would be central to the battle plan and therefore in total control of what advance or retreat may be determined on their side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: During your time, 1994, did you have an opportunity to observe how General Mladic interacted with his military subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We had many opportunities to see how he dealt with his subordinates. During our many meetings we had with him he was often accompanied by his subordinates, and they showed complete respect and clearly under total command of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of a situation in which anyone within the Bosnian Serb army acted contrary or in opposition to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bibles. We have another ten minutes left before the break, Mr. Lukic, but before I give you an opportunity to start your examination. Mr. Rose, you may be surprised to see only two Judges. One of the Judges, Judge Fluegge, is for urgent reasons unable to sit today. He will be with us tomorrow again and he has access to the full transcript and, if need be, even the audio and video of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you're ready. Mr. Rose, you'll be cross-examined now by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have a hard copy of your statement before you, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's just that I need to find one for myself. Let us go to paragraph 22. That's where we will start. There you say -- well, you discuss Dobrinja, saying that the area of Dobrinja was virtually surrounded. As a matter of fact, there was an exit across Mojmilo hill, whereby one could move between Dobrinja and the rest of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It could possibly be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja also had access to other parts of territory under Muslim control and that is proven by the fact that one side of the tunnel which went under the airport runway actually ended in Dobrinja. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The UN had no knowledge of the tunnel, official knowledge, at the time. Went to examine which areas were sounded and which areas were not, we would have to have a map in front of us. So I cannot make a valid comment on how much Dobrinja was surrounded or how much it was not surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you had no personal knowledge, official knowledge, of the existence of the tunnel. But, as a matter of fact, you were aware of its existence, were you not? No one could have been ignorant of its existence as long as they were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was certainly rumours to the effect that a tunnel existed, but the Bosnian government side kept the knowledge of its whereabouts to themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rose, may I ask you one clarification. Your answer was: "There certainly were rumours to the effect that the tunnel existed, but the Bosnian government side kept the knowledge of its whereabouts to themselves." These are two items, first the existence of a tunnel wherever --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- second, where it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did -- could I ask you to explain on both whether the Bosnian government also was silent on the existence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was silent on the existence of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
