utterances.text: And therefore would not reveal its whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your reports -- actually, in the reports you received from your subordinates and the reports you authored, did you mention the existence of the tunnel under the runway?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 23 of your statement you say: "The general view at this time, as I was briefed, was that there was indiscriminate shelling of civilians within the city centre by the Bosnian Serbs. A number of incidents which occurred immediately prior to my arrival and shortly afterwards supported that view. For example..." Actually, you go on to say that: "It is also the case that of course shelling was going the other way from time to time against the Bosnian Serbs," et cetera. "Sniping was also prevalent during this period, by both sides." UNPROFOR was unaware of the strength and structure or disposition of units, facilities, buildings, and commands of the 1st Corps of the BH Army in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, sorry to interrupt again but I'd like to seek clarification of the first line of paragraph 23. It starts: "The general view at this time, as I was briefed ..." Now, I'm not a native English-speaking person, but should I understand this "the general view at this time," the time when I was briefed or the general view at this time according to how I was briefed? Which of the two? And it may be that it's a wrong reading anyhow, that there's no ambiguity at all in the language, but could you please assist me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. As I arrived in Sarajevo in January 1994, I received, prior to arrival and after my arrival, many briefings. And the basis of those briefings were and the evidence were - anyway, was all around to see - that Sarajevo had been for two years under heavy shell fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so you're --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And continued to be under shell fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're both referring here to the content of the briefing and on what you observed at the time, although general view is difficult to observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, would you agree that if UNPROFOR was unaware of the disposition of units, facilities, buildings, and commands of the 1st Corps of the BH Army, it also could not have known what it was that the Serbs were targeting in Sarajevo, i.e., whether the shelling was random or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Again, putting that question in context, the United Nations' presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina was to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid. They were there by agreement with initially three warring parties. They were not there in a military capacity, therefore they did not have intelligence-gathering capabilities. They were working with, albeit recalcitrant parties to try and deliver humanitarian aid and to bring about peace. They were not in a position to have detailed military knowledge of the strength, deployments, intentions of any of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since in this paragraph there is a brief mention of snipers, on the 6th of October, 2010 -- well, could we please have 1D549 in e-court first. It is the transcript from the Karadzic case. We need page 17 in e-court. We need page 7336, lines 13 through 17. General, you see Judge Kwon's question there. He asked: [In English] "General, you can confirm what is stated in this information sheet; i.e., that you believe Ganic organised his secret police to snipe trams?" And your answer was: "That was certainly our belief at that time, sir, yes." [Interpretation] My question is this: Do you still stand by this part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time, as you say, there were three warring parties. During any of the briefings you received did anyone tell you that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina made up one-third of the population and that before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina they also enjoyed the right to one-third of all positions within the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That did form part of my briefing, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, looking at the clock. I do not know ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can break now. We'll take a break and we'll resume at quarter past 12.00 after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you're ready, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we continue, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, why did I ask you about the percentage of Serbs and their participation in power? Is it correct that UNPROFOR treated only the Bosnian or Muslim side as the official representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Serbs were at the time treated as rebels; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The United Nations had recognised the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992. They'd never recognised the existence of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] At that time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is it true - and you refer to that at page 7322 on the 6th of October, 2012, when you testified in the Karadzic case - that the Western powers did not understand the nature of conflict as it developed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I'd have to see that on the screen in context before I reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we please have in e-court 1D549. It should be page 41 in e-court. We need page 7322 -- actually, 73 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is -- the page you're mentioning is on e-court page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, obviously I stand corrected. Yes. We need the last row of this page -- actually, we need rows 16 to 19, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You'll see, General, on the screen it's saying: "Is that what I said, that that was an observation of yours, that there was a lack of understanding among Western governments, in terms of the nature of the conflict?" And your answer was: "That is true." Would you agree with this today as well, General?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask Mr. Lukic to understand what is -- what the witness is being asked to answer to. This question says -- is asking the witness whether is that what I said. And does the answer "that's true" answer to the fact yes that's what you said, or does it answer to the fact that there was a lack of understanding among Western governments? I'm not quite sure what he's being -- what the answer is responding to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, General, can you explain this issue to Your Honours -- to His Honour?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: My understanding today of that statement is that there were people in the West, NATO being America, who wished to use more force in resolving the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina than the United Nations felt was appropriate to a peacekeeping mission and that there was this misunderstanding about what a peacekeeping mission could do and what it could not do with regards to the use of force. And I think that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- reading it, it seems that you are -- that the parties were putting a part of your book to you in which certain language is used and that you're invited to confirm that that is what you -- your feelings or your thoughts were. Now, Mr. Lukic, for the Chamber to fully understand such an isolated item of the testimony, of course we would like to see also what the relevant pages in the book say so that we have the context. It's, I do understand, page 3 of the book which in the very beginning, so it might be an introductory observation. For the Chamber to fully understand this part of the testimony and the confirmation Mr. Rose has given today, the Chamber would like to have access to the previous pages, this was the third page of that day's session, perhaps the tow previous pages, and also the relevant portion of the book on which the witness then commented.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for us this is enough what General said today because we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but as I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we would like to have the context. We need to fully understand. If it's enough for you it doesn't mean that it's enough for us. Could you please prepare that we receive in evidence the previous two pages as well and that we -- I don't know to what extent we still need 92 ter confirmations for that or attestations, but to take care that the Chamber has the full context available of this portion of the testimony including relevant pages of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let us focus on paragraph 28 of your statement. There reference is made to humanitarian aid being distributed and brought in in different ways, primarily by airplane to Tuzla. There was a plan to open up the airport there so as to enable an easier delivery of humanitarian aid. You said that the airport was not opened even a year later, which is when you left Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say towards the end of this paragraph -- well, you say: "...President Izetbegovic was later to state that he was prepared to see 10.000 Bosnians die of starvation rather than accept a single Serb on Bosnian territory)." Is it correct that one of the main reasons for not re-opening the airport was that the Muslim side -- that there should be Serb controllers at the airport who would control the goings-on at the airport and what was being distributed from it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No, that's not precisely what the discussion was about. The Serb side wished to have inspectors, not controllers, to examine the air cargos being brought in to ensure there were no weapons being brought in to the Muslim side. So there were inspectors not controllers, and that's the objection that the Bosnian government had, they would not allow inspectors from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the difference, if you may, between a controller and an inspector?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, I controller would be controlling the entire flow of aid coming in to Tuzla. An inspector merely inspects what is happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the last two and a half minutes it was pure repetition of what is found already in paragraph 28, apart from additional confusion that was created by the difference between "controller" and "inspector." There's nothing new. Cross-examination is there to test the evidence and to bring new evidence which is relevant for your case, not to emphasise what you consider important or to repeat what is there already. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you believe the position of Alija Izetbegovic, as we've just heard, when he discussed a multi-ethnic Sarajevo which was a thesis put forth by the Muslim side at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I'm not sure which statement by President Izetbegovic you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have just read in your statement that he was prepared to sacrifice 10.000 Bosniaks to see them die of starvation rather than accepting a single Serb in Bosnian territory. And now I'm narrowing it down to Sarajevo. Is it true that the Muslim government in Sarajevo was basically not in favour of a multi-ethnic society? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was never evidence to that effect. The issue over the inspector at Tuzla was, I think, one of sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to keep focused Mr. Lukic? I think I understand what you'd like to ask the witness. The last part is: "... President Izetbegovic was later to state that he was prepared to see 10.000 Bosnians die of starvation rather than accept a single Serb on Bosnian territory )." I think what Mr. Lukic would like to know whether you believed President Izetbegovic to be serious in such a strong denial of any multi-ethnicity in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic I think when he made that statement was -- should have added "in this instance" on Serb territory -- on Bosnian territory. What he was saying: I would not accept any Serb inspector at Tuzla on Bosnian territory there. He was not making a wider statement regarding his views on multi-ethnicity in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is that what the question you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you were seeking an answer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, did you come by information that Serbs and Croats wanted to leave the part of Sarajevo that was under the control of Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We never had any evidence presented to us that either the Serbs or Croats wanted to leave, although I think maybe some Croats did leave without our knowledge. Because once the Federation was created, they were free to come and go; the Serbs of course were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now please take a look at paragraph 30 of your statement, the last portion or, in fact, the last sentence where it reads: "My concept of demilitarisation was that subsequent to a cease-fire, weapons would be withdrawn beyond a certain agreed point by both sides. President Izetbegovic was generally not in favour of demilitarisation."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Ganic, Salajdzic? In other words, the other top leadership within the Muslim lines, were they in favour of demilitarisation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: None of them were. Their view was that they were a sovereign nation recognised by the United Nations and they had every right to position soldiers where they wanted on their own territory and they would not accept demilitarisation. Of course they were also worried that demilitarisation would result in the freezing of the conflict line and become de facto an international border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will get to that and spend some more time on that issue, but at this point I'd just like to ask you this: Is it correct that the Muslim party was, in fact, interested in extending war operations and the war?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Sometime during 1994 I think that the Bosnian government side abandoned the peace process because they were being armed by the Americans and others and trained and were given hope of recovering their lost territory by force of arms. This was particularly advanced by the forming of the Federation, which tilted the strategic military balance against the Bosnian Serb side. So it was in their interest, as they saw it, to return to war. In my view, of course, that was a wholly mistaken view, that it would take decades before they were able to create sufficient military strength to recover their lost territory by force of arms. And we pointed that out repeatedly to President Izetbegovic and Vice-President Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want you to know that it's not that I'm not satisfied with your answer. I'm just waiting for the interpretation to end. Just this is to explain why I pause before I put the next question. And now paragraph 31, please. You state here: "The Bosnian Serbs were in favour of general demilitarisation that would begin with the general demilitarisation of Sarajevo." And: "They suggested that UNPROFOR place monitors on the heavy weapons on their side as a confidence-building measure and that this would be a start to working towards a cease-fire?" You've just explained a moment ago why the Muslims were against the cease-fire and the demilitarisation of Sarajevo, but at that time, did you have any specific information about what Mr. Warren Zimmermann had promised Alija Izetbegovic? Did UNPROFOR have any information about the type of agreement reached between the Americans and the Muslim government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We were never so informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the Croats, too, were in fact in favour of a cessation of hostilities and an end to the war at the time while you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Following the Washington Accord, I had very little dealings with the Croatian side and I have no knowledge of what their position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, because you said that you were aware of the fact that the Americans were arming the Muslim side, were you privy to any information or did you have any information where these weapons were coming from? Did you know whether the weapons were coming from Iran, the United States? So did you have any information about the source of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: None at all. And I should probably modify the word "aware." We were aware of the rumours that this was happening and there was some circumstantial evidence, for example, the Bosnian soldiers started to appear in modern American-style uniforms, but how this equipment was getting to -- into Bosnia-Herzegovina, we had no knowledge at all. Because of course NATO controlled the air-space and they were not passing any information pertaining to that to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not have -- you did not control the land roads either so you didn't know whether the weapons came in by road; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct. We were an organisation that was facilitating the delivery of humanitarian aid. We were not a military occupying power.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have in e-court document 65 ter 8137.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you know this type of document; correct? You recognise the format?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who sent this fax? Who sent this fax message and to whom? Can you tell from this? It says the 31st of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It looks as though it's a signal passing between Zagreb and Belgrade and I'm not, as far as I can see, on the distribution list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a surprise to me too, but I just wanted to show you that you did not get this information either. You hadn't received that fax, although it deals with a meeting between you, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, and General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 2 for the benefit of the General, to show that he, too, was a member of this -- in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we look at paragraphs 3 and 4 we see that this is in fact a reference to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct and that I was certainly at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 we see that it reads -- well, it says that you were the one who proposed that ways and means be provided to disengage and separate forces and that Dr. Karadzic was enthusiastic about this but doubted that the Muslim side would agree, as this ran counter to their international propaganda strategy of portraying Sarajevo as the martyr town. And it goes on that General Mladic's reaction was also positive, but he was more cautious and recommended a step-by-step approach. This is another instance where you proposed a cessation of hostilities in Sarajevo. Can you recall what the reaction of the representative of -- representatives of the Muslim authorities in Sarajevo was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I can't recall. It was nearly 20 years ago, but the -- my view now would be that they were -- would have been resistant to any such suggestion because that was characteristic of their position of the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Towards the bottom of the page we can see that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... interpretation, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- the airport in Tuzla is mentioned. And reference is made to legitimate Serb's concerns and that they have to be taken into account, and these concerns were that without inspectors the airport could be used for funneling in weapons but also because the Serbs were concerned that the Muslim side could down a UN plane and then blame that on them. As you sit here, can you recall what the outcome of these negotiations on the Tuzla airport was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The end result, as you have already described, was negative. We never made any progress with opening Tuzla airport during the year that I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 Dr. Karadzic proposes not just the re-opening of the Tuzla but also of the Banja Luka airport; in other words, an airport, too, that was under the control of the Serb forces. Was the Banja Luka airport ever open while you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to February 1994 and paragraph 35 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Lukic, I saw in the 92 ter statement that one page is missing of this report. What efforts were made - and I'm addressing you, Ms. Bibles - to get a complete picture of this meeting? I mean, just to say, Well, we have a -- we have the minutes but not all of it is not very satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, the short answer is that we don't know where the missing pages are. It -- the document itself reflects that it would be paragraphs 1 and 2 of the minutes that are missing. The witness in his statement verifies that what is present in this document is consistent with his recollection of the meeting itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was: What efforts were made to get the complete version? If you can't answer that question right away, we'd like to be informed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 35 you talk about the shelling of Dobrinja, a suburb of Sarajevo, and you say that you went to the site after the attack and that you ordered a crater analysis to be carried out and the results showed conclusively that the rounds had been fired by Bosnian Serb forces. Many ballistics experts will testify on this. And we have discussed at length the findings here, but let me ask you, first of all: Do you know that the -- that the findings have never been finalised, the conclusion as to what had happened had never actually been finalised?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It's particularly difficult to identify a precise firing point by crater analysis. When you have five mortar bombs in a particular line, you can certainly tell the direction. The distance may not be so easy to define. The more bombs, you have crater bombs, the easier it becomes. And certainly our view at the time was that it had come from the Serb side. Balance -- it was, as you say, a balance of judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know what the results of this analysis were? Do you know where these people obtained their information from and that they started this investigation 28 days after the incident? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were usually two levels of investigation. First of all, an immediate one carried out by the French army engineers who had a certain experience in this area; and then, secondly, there would be a more detailed investigation from a team from Zagreb. I cannot remember at this length of time when the team from Zagreb made an analysis or, indeed, whether it ever did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now pull up 1D548 in e-court. That is your evidence of -- from October 2010 and could we have page 69, please, in e-court. That should be 7309, the transcript page, from the Karadzic trial. We have the right page. Let's take a look at lines 4 to 7 and then 11 through 18. Have you read what your evidence was? And I will have a brief question about this once you've read it, and that is the following: UNPROFOR did not have good or modern up-to-date equipment and it wasn't easy to conclude where the fire had come from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We're talking about two periods of time, the time of the Markale bombing and the Dobrinja mortar bomb. There was no mortar-locating radar deployed. By the autumn the UN had deployed mortar-locating radars which of course gave a great deal of precision in identifying the firing point. At this time it was an imprecise art, as I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 36, General, of your statement you say, speaking of Dobrinja, in the penultimate sentence: "The Serbs had it completely surrounded and were firing directly down into the suburb such that residents were forced to live in their basements." General, is it true that Dobrinja was at the same time a very strong stronghold of the Muslim forces, almost a bunker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Dobrinja was surrounded on three sides and that there was no way the Serbs could capture that part of the settlement? Half of Dobrinja was under Muslim control and the other half by -- under Serb control. Would it have been possible had it not been so strongly fortified that the Serbs would not have been able to capture it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: As I've explained, the UN was not in a position to make detailed, strategic, or even tactical-level analysis as to the correlation of forces on the ground. As you already pointed out, the word "completely surrounded" may have been a little extreme because there was a route, a hidden route, through Dobrinja from the airport into the main part of Sarajevo but it was a very narrow route indeed. And effectively, Dobrinja was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja was close to Mojmilo hill or adjacent to it which was under Muslim control, and in fact Sarajevo was linked with Igman and the roads that went across Igman via Dobrinja - is that correct? - through the tunnel that ran across Dobrinja and then under the airport runway to the part that was under the control of Muslim forces, Bosnian Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: As I've said, we had no precise knowledge as to the hidden routes into Sarajevo at the time. And what you're saying could well have been the case, but of course there were other negotiations and deals where stuff came across the line without the knowledge of the UN and this would have been an example of one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were aware of the Igman routes that were also used by UNPROFOR; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that those routes were used by Muslim forces to supply their armed formations in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Not to our knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to paragraph 37. There you say: "On the following day, the 5th of February, 1994 ... there was a massacre in Sarajevo ... a single mortar shell had been fired onto the Markale market-place not far from the Presidency." Markale and the single shell will be the subject of many investigation expert testimony in this case by eye-witnesses and ballistics experts. I would rather not go into ballistics issues with you but I would make a connection between this paragraph and the next paragraph in your statement, paragraph 38, where you also stress that: "General Milovanovic sent a fax message offering to form a mixed commission of military experts to determine the provenance of the attack." The question is this: Such a commission was never established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it considered to establish a joint commission comprising representatives of the Serb-Muslim side and UNPROFOR? Was it considered at all, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I don't really recall, but if it had been suggested to the Bosnian government side they would certainly have refused to accept Serb analysts on their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There were two commissions established in this regard. One attended the scene straight away and the other arrived subsequently from Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the first investigation there were representatives of the Muslim authorities and they gathered evidence for the most part; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thus, the second commission arriving from Zagreb relied on the evidence gathered, or rather, immediately following the incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Again, that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know and did you object to the fact that parts of evidence went missing or were removed immediately following the initial, the first, investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I certainly remember discussing with the French engineers that they had not been able to get hold of all the material because the Bosnian government side had removed a number of items from the site before they arrived. Whether they subsequently got access to these items, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next you say in paragraph 40 of your statement, in the last sentence: "I suggested that we should take advantage of the situation and look towards introducing a 20-kilometre total exclusion zone (TEZ) for heavy weapons." It had to do with seizing the opportunity created by this event at Markale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that -- actually, let me ask you something about something before the total exclusion zone was introduced. Before that and afterwards, the balance in terms of number of personnel was in favour of the Muslim side. I don't know whether you were familiar with that piece of information. If you are not, please say so.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the demilitarisation of Sarajevo actually was supposed to encompass the withdrawal of all armed individuals as well from Sarajevo in order for Sarajevo to become an unarmed city, and is it also correct that the Muslim side would not accept that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think you're conflating two issues. The first issue was the removal of heavy weapons which was agreed but not adhered to by both sides; the second issue was the demilitarisation, which we have already discussed, was resisted by the Bosnian Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that this agreement on collecting weapons was not implemented, are you saying that it was not implemented at all or that some parts of it were not implemented, i.e., that some pieces were not handed over at collection points?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was certainly not implemented hundred per cent by either side. Both sides cheated on the agreement and hid heavy weapons within that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that issue later on in more detail, but while we're on this topic let me ask you the following: Serbs took, or rather, used the weapons from collection points when attacked by the Muslim forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That was the claim made by the Bosnian Serbs when they came to seize weapons back from the collecting points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was their assertion that they had no other weapons and therefore had to use the ones that were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That was the assertion. Of course it was more of a political act, I think, than a military one, particularly as we suspected they had hidden the affected weapons and could have used those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it not dangerous for the Serbs to use those weapons that were under the control of the UN? Did they not expose themselves to the danger of air-strikes by the NATO Alliance?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: They did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us discuss the demilitarisation of Sarajevo briefly, so we will leave the area of collecting heavy weapons. In paragraph 42, you say: "President Izetbegovic said he would never agree to the withdrawal of his infantry from Sarajevo ..." I'm trying to understand the following, and I would kindly ask for your explanation: Did UNPROFOR accept that position by President Izetbegovic and what were further actions by UNPROFOR? Was there any effort made towards demilitarisation or was it given up on?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We had to accept his position as it stood at that time, but we didn't relent on our efforts to try and demilitarise the situation which was a part of bringing about permanent peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever threaten President Izetbegovic with air-strikes against his forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that later on, when I will ask you whether you could bring that about in fact or not, but I'm afraid we are at the end of this part of our session and we need to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a suitable moment for you. It is approximately the time one hour after we restarted. We'll take a break and resume at 25 minutes to 2.00 but only after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would appreciate if you would stop your loud conversations when the Chamber enters the courtroom, Mr. Mladic. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I take advantage of this time to inform the Chamber of two things? I spoke with Mr. Lukic about RM009. Mr. Lukic's estimate is four hours for that witness and the Prosecution will reduce its examination by 15 minutes, so that's four hours and 15 -- 4 hours, 45 minutes for the witness. We'll wait for the Chamber to direct us as how we might take care of the schedule. And, Your Honour, with respect to P723, it's a public exhibit from yesterday, the first page of that exhibit indicates where the videolink was from and the Prosecution is requesting, since it has no evidential value to the case, that the Chamber order the court officer to remove that first page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Registry is hereby instructed to replace P723 by the same document without the first page. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, may we continue?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please focus on paragraph 43 of your statement. There you say you met with General Divjak, deputy commander of the BH Army. That is at the end of the paragraph, you continue: "... to discuss the cease-fire. Surprisingly, he also agreed to observe the cease-fire." Could we please have 1D549 in e-court. It is your testimony, General, of the 6th October 2010 in the Karadzic case in order to refresh your recollection. We need page 20 towards the bottom starting with line 14. We also need page 21, the first four lines just following this page. Please, can we go back to the previous page. My apologies. Let us go to page 20 so that the General would have sufficient time to read it. We see here, General, that you said that General "...'Divjak was reluctant to sign up to a cease-fire, once again on the grounds that the UN proposal was not linked to any long-term political settlement.'" And then we see that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it looks at first sight to be a quote. So this is part of a question and not -- perhaps we come to that, but you introduced it as "you said," but apparently it is "you wrote," as quoted by the accused in that case. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, following this introductory part you provided on the 6th October 2010, you discuss further that you told Divjak that the shell which hit Markale, the one that exploded on the 5th of February, 1994, came from the Muslim positions and that you were able to establish that. Automatically, he had a change of heart and signed up to the agreement. What was your impression? Did he know that indeed the shell had arrived from the Muslim positions? Or did he have doubts regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, clearly he thought that if that information went public it would be very damaging to the Bosnia-Herzegovina side. As I said previously, the initial investigation was incomplete, but that was the first view of the French analysts, that it could have well come from the Bosnian government side, i.e., been dropped off the building physically. But that view was later rescinded. It was useful in that time in the end, it proved that pressure was such on Divjak that he signed up to the idea that they should have a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We said we won't go into the technical details of this matter. General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to verify this and to be very precise. What is quoted as what you've written in the book is that the first investigation would reveal that it was fired from the Muslim side, whereas your testimony today is the initial investigation was incomplete and the first view of the French analysts was that it could have well come from the Bosnian government side. These two are not the same, at least the one is it comes from the Muslim side, the other one is it may have come from the Muslim side. Now, which is the accurate presentation? That the French analysts said it came from or that it may have come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my memory is certainly hazy on the subject, but I guess if I wrote in the book that they were definite initially about where it had come from, then that would have been the view I had at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Subsequently it is no doubt it became far less certain where the bomb had been fired from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, something came to my mind - addressing the parties - dealing with what the report would have stated, I take it that sooner or later we'll have all of that in evidence. The same is with the Dobrinja shelling on the 4th of February, to the extent not portions are already in evidence but forgive me for not having on my mind every single piece of evidence where there are so many reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The Chamber can look forward to additional evidence with respect to these reports, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, please look at paragraph 46 next, where you discuss the 12th of February, 1994: "General Milovanovic sent a fax protesting the Bosnian government breaches of the cease-fire ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D552 in e-court. We need --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see -- well, you can see it in English. It is a document of the SRK command. It's a regular combat report for the 9th of April, 1994, that is to say a few days -- well, in April. In the B/C/S we need page 2, whereas in the English version we need page 4. General, at the time did you have information that UN convoys were transporting weapons and ammunition for the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The allegation was often made, but to my knowledge the UN never moved weapons or ammunition for the Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here we see in this document that at around 8.30 p.m. on the 8th of April, 1994, a humanitarian aid convoy for the city of Sarajevo was searched, seven trucks and one jeep, during which a large quantity of ammunition for Brownings and medical material were found that were not on the list of goods to be transported. At the time were you informed of this incident or allegation by the SRK command?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: To my knowledge, I was never made aware of this supposed incident, and I'm sure I would have been made aware and I would have remembered it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please bear with me. Would you agree with me that the situation of the Muslim forces in 1994 improved drastically, not only due to the Washington Agreement but also because those forces were constantly receiving ever-larger amounts of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We certainly detected that the Bosnian government forces were improving their capability, but how they were doing that and where their ammunition or equipment was coming from, as I say, we had no direct knowledge. Our role there was purely to facilitate humanitarian aid, not to act as a guarantor of the arms embargo which of course was a responsibility of NATO, not ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move to March 1994. Kindly look at paragraph 55 of your statement. On the 1st of March, 1994, a framework Washington Agreement was signed creating the Federation of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. Nowhere in the documents was I able to find whether there was any contribution of yours to the signing of the Washington Agreement of the 18th of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I was the person that chaired the meeting near Zagreb where the two parties were brought together, and it was my wording that stood for that agreement, but of course it was a politically done deal. I merely had to administer the cease-fire, the signing of the cease-fire, and then the separation of forces, et cetera, which follows any end of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The territory controlled by Fikret Abdic, did it make part of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that Federation there was no clear delineation of which part of the territory belonged to which side, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was no clear delineation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The signing of this agreement followed shortly a period of fighting between Muslims and Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I don't recall whether it did. They certainly had been fighting during the time that I had been in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was one month roughly, maybe two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The fighting between Muslims and Croats for the most part took place in 1993 when you were not in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is probably why you're not aware of any details and we will gladly accept that. In paragraph 56, you say: "On the 3rd of March, 1994, I attended a meeting at Lukavica Barracks with General Mladic. At the meeting he proposed that there should be a meeting with the Bosnian government over the establishment of a global peace agreement." My question is: Is it true, is it correct, that it was neither the first nor the last time that such proposals arrived from General Mladic and the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 59 you discuss the 7th of March and the opening of the bridge over the -- at Grbavica. You said you "met with Dr. Ganic, Mr. Muratovic, General Delic, and Brigadier-General Karavelic at the Presidency. Agreement was reached over opening the Grbavica bridge ... as far as I know," the bridge, had been closed ever since the beginning of the war. Were there any problems on the Serb side with the opening of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No, the objections came from Mr. Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 61 next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I meanwhile ask a question, Mr. Lukic? You said that General Mladic had at very occasions proposed a -- or at least Bosnian Serb side had proposed a global peace agreement. Was that an open proposal: Let's agree on peace? Or was it related to the status quo? Or could you explain a bit more about how open that proposal was, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a very open proposal. It was a general proposal that was always on the table whenever we met with the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and without any conditions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or suggestions about the content?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just add on to what Judge Orie just said to ask you this: Irrespective of the reasons, was it your impression that the Serb side was honest in its proposals to end the war, it was sincere?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I'm sure they wished to end the war when they were at the most advantageous military and political position. And after 1994 I think they passed what Clausewitz would call the culminating point and that position was bound to deteriorate so therefore it was in their interest to seek and secure a peace at that time, in 1994. And of course events subsequently proved that assessment to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to explore a bit more the issue that Judge Orie has initiated. You said this was an open proposal. Does that mean that there were no preconditions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Depending on when you're talking about. At the time of the attack into Gorazde and its aftermath, then of course the Serb side wished the incident and the withdrawal of troops, et cetera, from around Gorazde to be part of the global agreement, whereas the Bosnian Serbs say that was a condition. But on the Bosnian government side, then they wished to be separate and be dealt with first before they moved on to any more long-term agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you agree with me that at the time while you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, almost all, if not all of, the offensive operations came from the Bosnian side and that this was the reason why the war continued?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think that would be too extreme a view. I think that there was attacks going on that we were possibly unaware of and elsewhere in Bosnia, not in the areas where we were deployed so I couldn't really make a substantive comment, but generally speaking the interests of the Bosnian Serbs was to secure peace and the interests of the Bosnian government side was to continue with the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, also Mr. Rose, I'm re-reading page 77, line 2 and following, especially on line 3 where it says that after "the attack into Gorazde, then of course the Serb side wished the incident and the withdrawal of troops, et cetera, from around Gorazde to be part of the global agreement, whereas the Bosnian Serbs say that was a condition." The "whereas" is confusing me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian government side wished to treat the Gorazde incident separately and deal with that before they moved on to discussion about a global agreement, whereas I think I'm correct in saying the Bosnian Serb side wished to just have a global agreement of which Gorazde would form a part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it was sequential in the case of the Bosnian government side but included within in part of the Bosnian Serb side and that was always the sticking point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, could we now please move on to paragraph 61 of your statement, that's another area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bihac namely. You state, and this is on the 12th of March, 1994: "The French Battalion in Bihac asked for an immediate air-strike against the Serb T55 tank that was firing at the headquarters of the Bosnian Army 5th Corps in the centre of town." Was there a request from NATO aviation to act as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The request to bring in air-strikes always came from the United Nations troops on the ground, never initiated by NATO. The only area in which NATO could fire a weapon without the authority of the United Nations was that of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did an air attack follow?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: On this occasion, not. A tank was moving in and out of cover and NATO were unable to identify that tank and engage it. So the mission was finally called off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to you, was the headquarters of the 5th Corps a legitimate target, military target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I guess in any war situation it would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So could NATO air-strikes against Serb positions be called for or requested even when the Serb positions targeted legitimate targets?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly, because they were firing into a built-up area and the enclaves were determined to be areas where fighting should not take place. The fact that the headquarters was located there didn't necessitate -- mean that they were necessarily fighting themselves, this is the Bosnian government side, in that area, in the built-up area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This came immediately after a Muslim attack against Serb positions and then in a counter-attack the Serbs pushed back the Muslim forces, and as part of that counter-attack they opened fire on the headquarters. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I don't think I can comment on that. All I remember is that a tank would come out of some cover, fire, and it seemed to be an isolated incident to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If the Muslim forces were to open fire from a built-up area at Serb positions would the Serbs be justified in that event to open fire at that particular point, even if it was in a built-up area? What was the UNPROFOR position?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR position of course was that no one should fire from a built-up area and engage -- and end up engaging the civilian population in combat, which is of course what happened far too many times in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I guess, as I say, in any war you have the right of return of fire and self-defence. But the response has to be proportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Talking about proportionality, we saw that, for instance, in the Afghanistan war, we saw British aircraft opening fire at a soldier carrying a Kalashnikov, opening fire with a 500-kilogramme bomb. Would that -- could that be called proportionate? And who is it that determines what proportionality actually entails? What military rules guide the decision as to what proportionality is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are giving an example from a different armed conflict, and you're asking, I think, the witness to write a thesis on many matters. Could you please focus the question, and I don't know whether you especially selected a British aircraft to fire on a soldier or not, but we are more interested in what happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. I see Mr. Mladic is seeking contact with counsel. The rules are clear about consultations, but if there's any specific matter we'll adjourn anyhow in four minutes. This could have been written down. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the last part of my question was actually what I wanted to ask: Where was that described what was proportionate? If the General can help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the proportionality principle, that's what you are referring to, Mr. Lukic, where you find the sources for that and the -- I take it also the considerations on what is proportionate and what is not proportionate. We have only three minutes left, Mr. Rose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, obviously each specific set of circumstances you have to make a judgement. But, for example, to call down an artillery barrage in Sarajevo against one mortar that had fired out at you would be disproportionate because you're inevitably going to cause unnecessary civilian casualty. If, for example, a mortar bomb was put on top of a hospital building and you called down fire and destroyed the hospital, that would be disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just get clarity, Mr. Rose. You're talking of a bomb on a hospital. It looks like you're including in this concept some kind of collateral damage. And I'm not quite sure whether you're talking about collateral damage or whether you're talking about proportionality. The example given of the British 500-tonne [sic] bomb was against a soldier with a Kalashnikov without any collateral damage around him. That would be a classic example, for me, of proportionality, of a discussion of proportionality. But once you put in there hospitals or protected people, you seem to introduce the concept of collateral damage and I'm not quite sure I understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm merely talking about collateral damage, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, the decision to waste a 500-pound bomb on an individual soldier, the end result is the same but that is disproportionate use from the tax payer's point of view. But if you're talking about law, the law of war, and you're talking about moral issues then you're talking about collateral damage. And the example I gave, again illustrative, if somebody put a single mortal tube on top of a hospital and fired one mortar bomb and you replied with an artillery barrage which caused a lot of civilian casualties, that would be disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I said we had three minutes left; they are gone now. Mr. Lukic, I am -- I think you have used approximately -- you've left a little bit over four hours of the time you claimed which was six hours, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked for seven, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked for seven. Which means we would not conclude the cross-examination tomorrow as matters stand now, but certainly in the first session of the day after that then I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day, Mr. Rose. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in the same courtroom, III. And I hope that you are prepared to stay for at least a part of another day with us, the day after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As long as it takes, sir, I shall be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's highly appreciated. Could -- I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever way about your testimony, irrespective of whether that is testimony you have given today or testimony still to be given the following days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fully understood, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 17th of January, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of January, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.15 p.m.,
